passage: Teacher's note, Class 4. Today Aditi, nine, told me something at recess. On Sunday her aunt knitted her a scratchy orange sweater. Aditi said, "I love it!" and hugged her. "But I don't love it," she whispered to me. "Did I lie?" She looked worried. We talked about how she wanted to be kind to her aunt, who knitted for weeks. I asked what else she could honestly say. She thought and said, "Thank you for making it for me." She smiled. I will read the class a story about kind honesty next week.

qa.q: What colour was the sweater Aditi's aunt knitted?
qa.a: Orange.

qa.q: Why did Aditi say she loved the sweater?
qa.a: She cared about her aunt and did not want to hurt her after all that work.

qa.q: What honest and kind option did Aditi find?
qa.a: Thanking her aunt for making it, which is both true and kind.

qa.q: How might the aunt feel if she heard Aditi's thank-you?
qa.a: She would likely feel appreciated for her effort.

grounding: It shows a child telling a kind white lie about a gift and learning that truth and kindness can pull apart.

passage: Dear Diary, Tonight Nani made her special kheer. It was really bland, like she forgot the sugar. But Nani was smiling so much and said it was her mother's recipe. So I said, "It's the best, Nani!" and ate it all. Now I feel a bit strange. I didn't want to hurt her, but it wasn't true. Mum said later that I could have said, "I love that you made Great-Nani's recipe." That's true. Maybe next time I'll say that. And maybe add sugar secretly.

qa.q: What did Nani make?
qa.a: Her special kheer.

qa.q: Why did the writer say the kheer was the best?
qa.a: To avoid hurting Nani, who was smiling and proud of her mother's recipe.

passage: In their village in Gujarat, eleven-year-old Hetal went with her family to her aunt's house for Diwali. She saw her aunt's hopeful face and said, "Yes, it's lovely." On the way home, she told her brother, "I felt bad saying that. But she looked so happy." Her brother said, "You could say thank you. That's true too." Hetal nodded.

passage: I'm Ishaan's older sister. Yesterday a glass broke in the kitchen. Ishaan, five, was standing right there. When Papa came running and shouted, "Who did this?", Ishaan pointed at our cousin Arjun and said, "Arjun did!" Arjun was in the other room. Ishaan's face was white and his hands were shaking. I don't know what was in his head, but he looked terrified, not sneaky. Later Mum knelt and said calmly, "No one will shout. Tell me what happened." He cried and said, "I did it. It slipped."

qa.a: A glass.

qa.a: Crumbs.

qa.q: Why did Riya say no biscuit?
qa.a: It was a hopeful reflex; she could not understand that her mother could see the crumbs.

qa.q: What did Mama do well?
qa.a: She stayed calm and showed Riya it is okay to say yes.

qa.q: How did Riya's brother react?
qa.a: He laughed at the crumbs on her face.

grounding: It shows a toddler denying eating a biscuit with crumbs on her face, a hopeful reflex, not cunning.

passage: Daycare note. At snack time today, Kabir, two, ate Tara's biscuit. When I asked, "Did you eat Tara's biscuit?" he said "No!" loudly, with crumbs all over his shirt. Tara cried. Kabir looked surprised that I did not believe him. I don't think he was being sneaky; he just hoped saying no would make it so. I said, "Let's say sorry and give Tara one." He did.

qa.q: What did Kabir eat?
qa.a: Tara's biscuit.

qa.q: Why was Kabir surprised he was not believed?
qa.a: He could not yet understand that the teacher could see the crumbs; his no was just a hopeful reflex.

qa.q: What did the teacher do well?
qa.a: She did not treat it as sneaky and guided Kabir to say sorry and share.

qa.q: How did Tara feel about losing her biscuit?
qa.a: She was upset and cried.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler's denial with visible evidence, a hopeful reflex rather than a plan.

passage: In a village home, two-year-old Pappu's grandmother found the jaggery jar open. "Pappu, did you eat jaggery?" Pappu shook his head. "No." His lips were sticky and brown. His sister giggled. The grandmother laughed too and wiped his mouth with her sari. "Sweet boy. Next time, just tell Dadi." Pappu grinned and pointed to the jar. "More?"

qa.q: What jar did the grandmother find open?
qa.a: The jaggery jar.

qa.q: Why did Pappu say no?
qa.a: It was a hopeful reflex; he did not understand that his sticky lips showed the truth.

qa.q: What did the grandmother do well?
qa.a: She stayed gentle and encouraged him to just tell her next time.

qa.q: How did Pappu's sister react?
qa.a: She giggled at the sticky, brown lips.

grounding: It shows a toddler denying eating jaggery with evidence on his face, a hopeful reflex.
